h: לְאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר אֲדָר רִאשׁוֹן, מַאֲמָר ב׳ For the Fourteenth of Adar Rishon — Maamar Bais

p: In the Shulchan Aruch at the end of Orach Chaim
Some say that one is obligated to increase
on the fourteenth of Adar Rishon,
but the practice is not so;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יַרְבֶּה קְצָת בִּסְעוּדָה וְכוּלֵּי
nevertheless one should increase somewhat in the meal...
"and one of good heart has a constant feast."
And in the sefer Birkei Yosef (se'if katan 2),
cited in the Shaarei Teshuvah (se'if katan 2),
he noted that the Rema, of blessed memory,
opened at the head of his glosses
and sealed with "and one of good heart has a constant feast,"
and he wrote an allusion on this.
The matter is that "Orach Chaim," the path of life,
means the way to acquire eternal life,
that in the words of Torah the term "life"
has a world of his own,
a share in the World to Come" (Sanhedrin 90a);
and the Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim
is the way to merit eternal life.
For thus death is called like sleep,
as is usual in the language of Chazal:
"And when you awaken, it will converse with you" (Mishlei 6:22) —
that through words of Torah it will help,
that since he will suffer only for a moment
the pain of death because of the blemish of the serpent,
he will then immediately merit eternal life,
and it will be only like one who goes to sleep
וּפָתַח בַּשֻּׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ [סִימָן א סְעִיף א]
The Shulchan Aruch (siman 1, se'if 1) opens with
"One should strengthen himself like a lion...,"
for the main thing is to overcome the yetzer hara
to rise in the morning for the service of his Creator;
וְהוּא כְּעֵין מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת טז, ב)
and this resembles what they said (Berachos 16b):
"May we rise early and find our hearts longing
meaning that without any preparation or effort
for the fear of Heaven and His service.
עַל זֶה פָּתַח הָרַמָּ״א זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה
therefore the Rema, of blessed memory, opened with
(ibid.) "I have set Hashem before me always":
that there should always stand before his eyes
that he picture that the King of the kings of kings,
the Holy One, blessed is He,
stands over him and sees his deeds,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִזְכֶּה לְיִרְאַת ה׳
and through this he will merit fear of Hashem
Afterward comes the order of the day,
through washing the hands and berachos
Afterward comes the order of the seasons,
and it opens with the laws of Shabbos (simanim 242–395)
which are the two roots of the sanctities of the times;
for the sanctity of Shabbos serves
to bring holiness into the six weekdays,
so that everything be in holiness.
for it is the head of the entire month,
so in Rosh Chodesh are contained
all the sanctities of the month,
and from it they radiate to all the days of the month.
Afterward it opens the festivals with Pesach,
for in the month of Nissan, first of the months of the year
Yisrael then merited all the light,
at the plague of the firstborn,
and afterward at the splitting of the Yam Suf;
רַק דְּאַחַר כָּךְ נִסְתַּר הָאוֹר מֵהֶם
only that afterward the light was hidden from them,
the time of the giving of our Torah (siman 494),
and Sukkos, the time of our rejoicing
which is the time to merit the complete rectification
and the Shulchan Aruch concludes with the month of Adar
We have already said, from the sefer Kedushas Levi
דְּחָשַׁב חֹדֶשׁ אֲדָר נֶגֶד שֵׁבֶט יוֹסֵף
that he counted the month of Adar as corresponding to the tribe of Yosef,
וְעַל כֵּן מִתְחַלֵּק בִּשְׁנַת הָעִיבּוּר לִשְׁנַיִם
and therefore it divides in a leap year into two,
מְנַשֶּׁה עַל שֵׁם כִּי נַשַּׁנִי וְגוֹמֵר [בְּרֵאשִׁית מא, נא]
Menasheh, named for "For God has made me forget..." (Bereishis 41:51),
which is the time of the eradication of Amalek,
as they said in the holy Zohar
and Ephraim, from whom came Yehoshua,
who gave Eretz Yisrael to Yisrael as an inheritance,
שֶׁהִיא שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשַּׁת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
which is the root of the holiness of Torah she'b'al peh;
and this is what they said (Nedarim 22b)
that it is the inventory of Eretz Yisrael;
וְאַחַר כָּךְ יֵצֵא מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן יוֹסֵף מִזַּרְעוֹ
and afterward Mashiach ben Yosef will come from his seed,
who will rectify all of Yisrael
through the revelation of the depth
the abundance of wisdom that will rectify the abundance of anger,
And this is why the Rema concluded,
in the manner of the opening,
"and one of good heart has a constant feast,"
to allude: "good of lev," not levav,
meaning that there should be only one heart
if he is worthy, it gladdens him;
for merit is needed for this,
that it "gladden the heart of man."
And the month of Adar is the time
to merit the light of Torah she'b'al peh,
שֶׁהוּא שְׁתוּ בְּיַיִן מָסָכְתִּי [מִשְׁלֵי ט, ה]
which is "drink of the wine I have mixed" (Mishlei 9:5),
the wine of the Oral Torah
and he will be "of good heart, a constant feast" —
the wine of the Oral Torah.
For in Adar "they accepted it anew
as they said in Midrash Tanchuma
And this is what they said (Pesachim 68b):
would sit fasting the whole year
in the name of the Ri
that it speaks of a dream fast,
even though on Shabbos it is permitted.
The reason is that the dream fast
is to tear up his decree,
and on Purim the feasting and rejoicing
because then there began to sprout
the expansion of Torah she'b'al peh,
which is "the wine I have mixed,"
the wine of the Oral Torah,
וְנִרְמָז וְטוֹב לֵב עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
And "good of heart" alludes to words of Torah,
that he occupied himself with words of Torah;
up to here, regarding words of Torah;
and in the manner they said (Berachos 5a):
"For I have given you good teaching...,"
וְכֵן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִקְרָא טוֹב
and likewise Torah she'b'al peh is called "good,"
"The Torah of Your mouth is good for me...,"
and this is the obligation constantly.
"and one of good heart has a constant feast" —
this is the master of Mishnah;
that this is the master of Gemara.
וְעַל כֵּן דָּרַשׁ עַל זֶה וְטוֹב לֵב
and therefore he expounded "good of heart" about it,
for this is the main thing in learning,
"He has set me in dark places" (Eichah 3:6) —
this is the Talmud of Bavel.
for through pilpul, one who merits
brings forth buds and blossoms for the words of Torah,
these are the talmidei chachamim in Bavel,
who make buds and blossoms for the Torah;
and on the contrary, through this
those who toil in Torah she'b'al peh,
on the pasuk, "The people who walk in darkness
the light that was created on the first day....
"and one of good heart has a constant feast,"
that words of Torah should be absorbed in him,
for this is the constant obligation,
"and you shall meditate in it day and night";
and he began his glosses with the fear of Hashem,
"The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem,"
and this too is an obligation constantly,
"I have set Hashem before me always."

paragraphs.text: Rema, Orach Chaim 1:1 — “I have set Hashem before me continually: this is a great principle in Torah and in the virtues of the righteous who walk before God. A person's sitting, movements, and dealings alone in his house are unlike his sitting, movements, and dealings before a great king. ... When he takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, fear, submission, and shame before God will immediately reach him.”

paragraphs.text: Shaarei Teshuvah 697:2, quoting Birkei Yosef — “See Birkei Yosef, who wrote that our master Rema, of blessed memory, wisely established a conclusion corresponding to his opening: two continual offerings in their order. He began his glosses with I have set Hashem before me continually, and concluded with One of good heart has a continual feast.” This verifies the Birkei Yosef observation through Shaarei Teshuvah, the intermediary explicitly cited by Rav Tzadok; it does not claim independent collation of Birkei Yosef's printed page.

paragraphs.text: Sotah 21a — “Torah is compared to light, to tell you: just as light protects continually, so Torah protects continually. It says, When you walk, it shall guide you: this is this world. When you lie down, it shall guard you: this is death. When you awaken, it shall converse with you: in the future to come.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 20 — “One who merits to be engraved on the Tablets does not die … and it is written, ‘When you awaken, it will converse with you’ — in the time to come.” This names the condition for such a death. Torah that frees a person from the yetzer hara makes death a passing sleep, which is the life the “Orach Chaim” leads to.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 16b — “May it be Your will, Hashem our God, to make love, brotherhood, peace, and friendship dwell in our lot. ... Set our portion in Gan Eden and establish for us a good companion and a good inclination in Your world. May we rise early and find our hearts' hope directed to fearing Your Name; may the satisfaction of our souls come before You for good.” These are part of Rabbi Elazar's words after prayer. Rav Tzadok interprets the heart's readiness at waking as an initial Divine gift.

paragraphs.text: Eruvin 41a — “After Rabban Gamliel died, Rabbi Yehoshua entered to overturn his ruling. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri stood and said: I see that the body follows the head! Throughout Rabban Gamliel's life we established the law according to him; now you wish to overturn his words? Yehoshua, we do not heed you, for the law has already been established according to Rabban Gamliel, and no one disputed the matter.” The proverb occurs in a dispute about maintaining an established ruling after a leader's death. Rav Tzadok applies its image to Rosh Chodesh as the head that directs the month.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Iyar 1 — “The main light of the month is included in Rosh Chodesh … for it is the head of the month, and all follows the head.” Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why Iyar is called “Ziv”: its Rosh Chodesh was the first after the Avos were born in Nissan, so their radiance is credited to it.

paragraphs.text: Kiddushin 49b — “Ten measures of wisdom descended to the world: the Land of Israel took nine, and the whole world took one. Ten measures of beauty descended to the world: Jerusalem took nine, and the whole world took one.” The first statement grounds Rav Tzadok's association of the Land with Torah wisdom. The measure is the Gemara's figurative language, not a numerical survey.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 76b — “Rava raised a contradiction: it is written yeshammach and read yesammach. If he merits, wine gladdens him; if he does not merit, it devastates him. This is what Rava said: Wine and spices have made me perceptive.” The wordplay distinguishes beneficial joy from wine's ruinous effect. Rav Tzadok applies the requirement of merit to the spiritual wine of Oral Torah.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 68b — “Mar son of Ravina fasted throughout the year, except for Shavuos, Purim, and the eve of Yom Kippur. Shavuos is the day on which Torah was given. Concerning Purim it is written, Days of feasting and joy. Concerning the eve of Yom Kippur, Chiyya bar Rav of Difti taught: Whoever eats and drinks on the ninth, Scripture accounts it to him as if he had fasted on the ninth and tenth.”

paragraphs.text: Tosafos, Berachos 49b, s.v. I bai achil — “That which is said in Pesachim, that Mar son of Ravina fasted throughout the year, implies that he fasted on festivals. Ri explains that the passage concerns a fast over a dream; other fasts are forbidden.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shavuos 12 — “Tosafos say it was a dream fast… except on Purim, where the term ‘feasting’ is used … and on Atzeres the eating is like a korban, which is the main intent of a fast.” Here Rav Tzadok gives a second reason for Mar bar Ravina's exceptions. On these three days the eating itself fulfills what a fast is meant to accomplish.

paragraphs.text: Ruth Rabbah 5:15 — “‘Boaz ate and drank, and his heart was good.’ Why was his heart good? He blessed over his food. Another interpretation: His heart was good because he ate sweet foods after the meal, which accustom the tongue to Torah. Another interpretation: His heart was good because he engaged in words of Torah, as it is said, ‘The Torah of Your mouth is better for me.’ Another interpretation: His heart was good because he sought a wife, as it is said, ‘One who has found a wife has found good.’” The Midrash gives several explanations of Boaz's glad heart. Rav Tzadok follows the explanation that identifies the gladness with Torah.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 63b — “Reish Lakish said: Up to here the verse concerns words of Torah; from here onward it concerns good deeds.” The verse begins, Rejoice, young man, in your youth, and let your heart gladden you. Reish Lakish reads its first portion as encouragement in Torah and its latter portion as a demand for action.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 5a — “Rabbi Yochanan said: ... Whoever can occupy himself with Torah but does not do so, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings ugly sufferings upon him and troubles him, as it is said, I became mute in silence; I was silent from good, and my pain was stirred up. Good means nothing other than Torah, as it is said, For I have given you a good teaching; do not abandon My Torah.” Rav Tzadok draws on the identification of good with Torah when reading a good heart as a heart shaped by Torah.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 145b — “Rabbi Zeira said in Rav's name: What is meant by All the days of a poor man are bad? This is the master of Talmud. One of good heart has a continual feast: this is the master of Mishnah. Rava said the opposite. Rav Mesharshiya said in Rava's name: One who moves stones is pained by them refers to masters of Mishnah; one who splits wood benefits through it refers to masters of Talmud.” Rav and Rava assign the glad heart differently. Rav Tzadok preserves both: settled rulings guide practice, while successful Talmudic analysis discloses fresh Torah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Divrei Soferim 36 — “Of them they said in Tanchuma that there is great pain and sleeplessness, likened to darkness … this is the Talmud of Bavel; for Talmud is the delving into the depths of Torah.” Rav Tzadok explains the “darkness” of the Bavli as its depth. Those sunk in that depth become people whose every word is Torah.
